appraisal_events.evidence: Kept again late in life by the proud old duke, Odette 'diminishes herself' seeking only the dressing-gowns and dishes he likes and flattering his friends, tending despite all her acquired social position to become again 'the lady in pink'; meanwhile nephews and duchesses hoping for an inheritance or to spite Oriane now flock to her.
appraisal_events.explanation: Odette's personal dignity is narrated as regressing to her old kept-woman role even as, ironically, her social traffic increases through the duke's patronage and others' opportunism.

appraisal_events.evidence: The duke's affair with Mme de Forcheville costs him, for the second time, the presidency of the Jockey Club and a seat at the Academie des Beaux-Arts, just as M. de Charlus's life, publicly linked to Jupien, cost him the presidency of the Union and of the Societe des amis du Vieux Paris -- 'the two brothers... had arrived at discredit.'
appraisal_events.explanation: Both brothers' scandalous attachments are narrated as costing them concrete institutional prestige, an explicit, witnessed social discredit.

appraisal_events.evidence: Odette, 'entirely taken up with younger suitors, was mocking him' during his brief visit to see her.
appraisal_events.explanation: The duke who dominates and sequesters Odette is nonetheless privately mocked by her, undercutting him within the very relationship he controls.

appraisal_events.evidence: Once 'almost ridiculous' playing the stage king, the ravaged old duke is now described as having taken on 'a truly grand' aspect, resembling his brother, made by old age 'august, suppliant' rather than merely pitiful -- 'more than a ruin, that beautiful romantic thing a rock can be in a storm.'
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator elevates the duke aesthetically and morally in his physical decline, finding in his ruin a tragic dignity he lacked in his prouder days.

status_effects.explanation: The narrator frames her catering to the duke's whims as a personal self-diminishment back toward her old kept-woman role.
Despite the personal diminishment, her social traffic visibly increases as opportunistic relatives and rival duchesses now seek her out.
He concretely and publicly loses two prestigious institutional positions because of his scandalous liaison.
His public association with Jupien is cited as costing him two presidencies, a further institutional discredit.
He is privately mocked by the very mistress he dominates and sequesters.
The narrator's tragic, admiring portrait of his physical ruin confers a dignity he did not have in his formerly ridiculous pride.
